title: Christ's questions to Saul and the types of himself
english: Of what first honors have I deprived you? Did I close paradise to you? Did you put on the leaves of the fig tree because of me? Did I become the cause of your turning back to the earth? Did you fall from your rule, cut short your inheritance, and diminish the image because of me?

“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). You had the Law, and I, as the good one, added grace. You were laboring over the letter, and I presented the Spirit. The shadows were grieving you, and I came forward and showed the truth. You were stumbling over the types, and I brought one remedy in place of many—the moneyless one in place of the money-lovers. I interpreted the Sabbath for you and gave it glory. I stopped the wound of your circumcision. I freed the altar from groanings, and in place of the much-groaned sacrifices I showed the ever-joyful, the un-groaning one.

“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). Be ashamed before Abraham’s tent, and remember the altar of Isaac; take up in your memory the wrestling of Jacob. Why have you handed over Joseph’s dreams to forgetfulness? How does the rod of Moses not shame you, or the sheepskin of Elijah, or the courage of Elisha? These are types of me; their prophecies are about me.

“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). I showed Jeremiah the almond rod; I painted the golden lampstand for Zechariah; I pointed out to Daniel the stone cut without hands; I widened the belly of the sea monster for Jonah; the great Ezekiel saw me as the charioteer of the cherubim; I am the much-spoken-of sheep of Isaiah.

“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). Consider where you aim your bows: “For heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” (Isaiah 66:1). Where are you sending your arrows? “For I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). At whom are you throwing stones? I “measured the water in my hand and the heaven with a span and all the earth with a handful” (Isaiah 40:12). Against whom are you arming your tongue? I make clear the tongues of those who speak with difficulty; I made the deaf and the mute; I fashioned the seeing and the blind. See whom you call a deceiver: “I multiplied visions and was likened in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea 12:10).

“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). For David sings of me, but you revile me; he hymns me, but you blaspheme; he plays the lyre, but you kick; he plucks the strings, but you use weapons. “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4).

orientation: Christ continues speaking from heaven to Saul on the road, pressing him with rhetorical questions and then showing that the Law's types and the prophets were all about himself.

title: Christ questions Saul; Paul answers with faith
english: Why do you make war on me with my own gifts? You fight in defense of the Law, yet you campaign against me; you run for my sake, yet you punish my own people. You avenge my glory, but you do not know where the battle should be joined or where the war should be waged.”

These things Christ says to Saul, and Saul answers and says, “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 9:5). Paul’s zeal is good, because when he was called he obeyed at once. He received the word and immediately perceived the dignity of the one speaking, and he said, “Who are you, Lord? For I have been filled with the radiance, I have been captured by the light, I have become a prisoner of the ray. “Who are you, Lord?” I long to see your beauty; I am eager to fly up to the clouds; I desire to learn whence comes this “radiance of glory” (Hebrews 1:3), who is the “exact imprint of God’s being” (Hebrews 1:3), who is this one “sustaining all things by the word of his own power” (Hebrews 1:3). “Who are you, Lord?” I have heard your voice, and I have had my fill of the Law; no longer do I long for the Law, no longer do I wish for an ark of gilded wood; I long for a pure manger, wholly royal and honored with gifts of gold.” Let the children of all the heretics be put to shame, and let the mouths of the heretics be put to shame. For see, when Paul was called he does not busy himself with many questions, but only believes; he worships and does not fight; he sings hymns, and faultfinding has been removed. “Who are you, Lord?” he says. He would not have called him Lord if he had not perceived that the one calling him was God. The one he knew as God he confessed as maker; the one he confessed as maker he proclaimed as impassible; he held him as incorruptible. He worshiped as immortal the one whose cross he knew and whose tomb he recognized. He was not ignorant of the blows, the spear in the side, the slaps.

But what does Christ say to him in reply? “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you persecute” (Acts 22:8). He receives a concise answer to his question: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you persecute.” I am Jesus, the one who was and who is now, the one before all things and after all things, the one in the beginning and at the last times, the son of David yet himself before David, the maker from Abraham, the one from Adam yet himself the one who fashioned Adam, from Isaac yet himself the one who crowned Isaac’s altar, from Jacob yet himself the one Jacob saw on the ladder, surrounded by the hosts of angels. “I am Jesus, whom you persecute,” but in persecuting you do not overtake me; for where or how will you hunt “the radiance of glory” (Hebrews 1:3)?

title: Christ's rhetorical questions to Saul and Paul's transformation
english: What net can contain “the exact imprint of God’s being” (Hebrews 1:3)? Who can lay a hand on “the one who bears all things by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3)? “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” I keep you as the bridal escort of my bride. Why do you persecute me, the one for whom you will shortly be persecuted? But you wear out your feet in vain, you sweat for nothing, you labor uselessly; the one you are persecuting sits in the Father’s bosom. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” not knowing that you are fighting against your own life. Why do you make war on the wise one? You wound a benefactor such as you have no other; you kick the nourisher for whose sake the earth without hesitation makes the table of fruits spring up for you. You despise the Savior, who, if he clenches his hand, who will free you from your sins? Who will release you from your bonds? In whose possession will you find the certificate of debt?”

So then this Paul, once a persecutor, is now an evangelist; once a pirate, now a pilot; once a wolf, now a shepherd; once lead, now gold; once a blasphemer, now speaking well and spoken well of by all. He is a leader among teachers, exceptional among the God-bearing, clear among prophets, wiser among apostles, unwounded among athletes, more glorious than the heralds of truth, more powerful than the soldiers of piety. For who “was beaten with rods three times” and prayed for a fourth? Who “five times received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one” (2 Corinthians 11:24-25), as he boasts? Who, “having spent a night and a day in the deep” (2 Corinthians 11:25), presents the shipwreck instead of a bridal bath, “often in journeys” (2 Corinthians 11:26) but making all of them profitable, each one richly profitable? Who faced “dangers from robbers, dangers from his own people, dangers from rivers, dangers in the wilderness, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers among false brothers” (2 Corinthians 11:26), and did not scatter the wealth of his endurance? Who carries the care of all the churches, yet is not constrained by the experience of burdens, nor are his shoulders weighed down, nor does he bend his back? Who then so detests sin, yet has such compassion for sinners? No one. For he always intercedes that we may obtain eternal good things, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
translator_notes: The number 'five times forty minus one' is a direct allusion to the Johannine count of the disciples/works.
The digit '3' at the end of the text is an edition/page marker and was skipped.
